questions.q: "Create a task" exists as an HTTP route, an RPC procedure and a queue job, each written separately. What is the problem the lesson points out?
questions.explain: Logic written three times is changed three times, and sooner or later one copy is missed. An operation holds the rules once; each transport only translates.
options: The copies drift apart: one forgets the title check, another returns a different error
HTTP and RPC cannot share a database
A queue job cannot create tasks

questions.q: In @zudojs/api, what is a transport's job?
questions.explain: A transport is the door a call comes through. It finds the operation, builds a context from what it verified, calls the executor, and translates the result. The rules live in the operation.
options: To hold the business rules, such as the title check
To translate: turn an HTTP request, RPC frame or queue job into an operation call, and the result back into its own answer

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: defineOperation checks the definition at once, so a bad name fails when the program starts, not on the first request. Names use letters, digits and signs like ., as in tasks.create.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every operation has a timeout, and it cannot be switched off with 0. A bad timeout is refused when the operation is defined.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The executor wraps every answer in a result: { ok: true, data }. The handler got the cleaned input, so the spaces around the title were trimmed by the schema.
options: { ok: true, data: { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false } }
{ ok: true, data: { id: 1, title: '  Buy milk  ', done: false } }
{ success: true, result: { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false } }

questions.q: How do you find out whether executor.execute(...) failed?
questions.explain: Every call gives back a result. With ok you cannot forget the failure case: TypeScript only lets you read data after checking ok.
options: Wrap it in try/catch; it throws on failure
Check result.ok: the executor never throws and returns { ok: false, error } on failure

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A bad input fails with 422. The issue says where the problem is (title) but not what was sent. The executor leaves the value out on purpose.
options: false 400 [ 'title: String must be at least 3 characters' ]

questions.q: Why do the executor's validation issues say only title: invalid and not the value that was sent?
questions.explain: An error message goes back to the caller and often into logs. Repeating the input there can leak a password typed into the wrong field. The path alone is enough to fix the request.
options: Schema messages often repeat the value, and that value can be a password or other secret
Because the value was already deleted
Because issues are only for logs

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: APIConflictError is a ready-made API error with status 409. The handler's own API error comes through unchanged, with its status and message.
options: 409 A task called "Buy milk" already exists.
500 An unexpected internal error occurred in operation "tasks.create".
422 A task called "Buy milk" already exists.

questions.q: You call executor.execute(createTask, { titel: "Buy milk" }, context) in a .ts file. What happens?
questions.explain: createTask is typed as APIOperation<NewTask, Task>, so TypeScript checks the input you pass. Inside transports the input is unknown, and the schema checks it at runtime.
options: The call returns a 422 at runtime, and that is the first you hear of it
TypeScript reports an error before the program runs, because titel is not in the input type
The handler receives undefined for the title and no one notices

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An error that is not an API error becomes an APIInternalError with a fixed message and expose: false. The database message, with its table and host, stays on cause for your logs.
options:
500 false
An unexpected internal error occurred in operation "tasks.export".

422 false
An unexpected internal error occurred in operation "tasks.export".

questions.q: Continuing from the internal error: what does this print?
questions.explain: The original error is kept on cause, which is good for logs. But turning the whole error into JSON includes that cause, so res.json(result.error) would leak it. Always pick the fields a caller may see.
options:
An unexpected internal error occurred in operation "tasks.export".
false

questions.q: What does expose: false on an API error mean?
questions.explain: expose is the flag that matters when you build a response. true means "safe to show to the caller"; false means "log it, send something generic".
options: Its message is not safe to show: log it, and send the caller a generic message
The error is thrown instead of returned

questions.q: The HTTP binding serves an operation whose handler crashes with a database message. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every binding sends failures in the same safe shape, { code, message, statusCode, requestId, issues? }. The message is hidden because the error is not exposed, and neither the cause nor the stack leaves the process. The request id lets a user quote the failure to support.
options:
500 false
{
  code: 'ERR_API_INTERNAL',
  message: 'An internal error occurred.',
  statusCode: 500,
  requestId: 'web-7'
}

500 true
{
  code: 'ERR_API_INTERNAL',
  message: 'relation "tasks" does not exist (host 10.0.0.5)',
  statusCode: 500,
  requestId: 'web-7'
}

200 false
{
  code: 'ERR_API_INTERNAL',
  message: 'An internal error occurred.',
  statusCode: 500,
  requestId: 'web-7'
}

500 true
{
  code: 'ERR_API_INTERNAL',
  message: 'An internal error occurred.',
  statusCode: 500,
  requestId: 'web-7',
  cause: 'relation "tasks" does not exist (host 10.0.0.5)'
}

questions.q: What does an API context carry through one call?
questions.explain: createAPIContext(requestId, state, signal) makes it. Typed slots are read and written with keys made by createContextKey, such as the built-in UserIdContextKey.
options: The database connection and the HTTP response
A request id, an optional cancel signal, a state object you choose, and typed slots

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The request id and state come from createAPIContext. The plan was set with its key. Nobody set UserIdContextKey, so it is undefined: an anonymous call.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A safe id is kept. The id with a line break is replaced by a fresh UUID (36 characters), so the fake log line never reaches your logs.

questions.q: What is log injection, and how does the lesson prevent it?
questions.explain: The x-request-id header is written by the client. Passed through normalizeRequestId, a safe id is kept and anything else becomes a fresh UUID.
options: Too many log lines; prevented by a log level
A caller puts a line break in a value such as x-request-id to add fake lines to your logs; normalizeRequestId replaces unsafe ids
Logs written in the wrong order; prevented by interceptors

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: createAPIContext refuses an unsafe id with a TypeError. That is why a transport passes header values through normalizeRequestId first.

questions.q: What is an interceptor in @zudojs/api?
questions.explain: It works like middleware. call holds the operation, the input and the context. It can also answer early without calling next(), by returning apiFailure(error).
options: A function that replaces the executor
An object with intercept(call, next): do something, await next(), do something after
A schema that runs after the handler

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first interceptor in the list is the outermost. That is why a logging interceptor placed first also sees the answers of the interceptors after it.
options: log in > auth > handler > log out
auth > log in > handler > log out
log in > log out > auth > handler
handler > auth > log in > log out

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The anonymous call is answered early with apiFailure, without next(), so the handler does not run. Ada has a user id in the context, so her call goes through: one handler run.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: freeze() locks the registry, so nobody can add or replace an operation while requests run. get returns undefined for an unknown name, and findByTag finds operations by their metadata tags.

questions.q: In the HTTP transport, where does the user id in the context come from?
questions.explain: Only identity the transport verified goes into the context. A user id in the body is written by the caller and proves nothing.
options: From a userId field in the JSON body
From the bearer token, after the transport checked it (here with a users map standing in for sessions or JWT)

questions.q: A caller with a guessed token posts an invalid title to the HTTP binding. Why does it get 401 and not the 422 with the validation issues?
questions.explain: Because the interceptors come first, an unknown caller never learns what a valid input looks like. Only a signed-in user's invalid call gets the 422 with its issues.
options: The binding checks tokens itself before it looks at any operation
Interceptors run before the input is checked against the schema, so requireUser refuses the call first
Invalid titles are always answered with 401
The schema is turned off for unknown callers

questions.q: In registerApiRpcProcedures, where must the state function take the user id from?
questions.explain: Metadata, the frame's id and the payload are all written by the caller. Only call.auth, filled in by the transport's auth option after a check, says who the caller really is.
options: From call.auth, the identity the RPC transport verified

questions.q: The queue transport adds jobs with { attempts: 1 }. Why?
questions.explain: Retries help with errors that can go away, like a restarting service. An invalid input stays invalid. After the failure, the queue's dead-letter rules take over.
options: The queue cannot retry API operations
A validation error fails the same way every time, so retrying it only wastes work
It makes the job run faster
So a job runs once per user

questions.q: A background job has no HTTP request and no token. Why may the queue binding's state take the user id from job.metadata.userId?
questions.explain: The trust comes from who writes the metadata. Jobs are added by your code after it verified the user. Never let a client choose a job's metadata: whoever writes userId there acts as that user.
options: Only your own code adds jobs, after it has checked who the user is, so the id is as trusted as that check
Any client may set it, and that is fine for background work

questions.q: An operation's timeout runs out while its handler is still working. What does the executor do?
questions.explain: JavaScript cannot stop a running function from outside, so the executor aborts the signal with the same APITimeoutError the caller got. Pass context.signal to fetch or database calls, or check it in a loop.
options: It answers the caller with ERR_API_TIMEOUT (504) and aborts the handler's context.signal, so a handler that passes the signal on or checks it stops
Nothing: the caller waits until the handler finishes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After 50 ms the executor aborted the handler's signal with the same APITimeoutError the caller got, so the sleep rejected at once and the handler stopped instead of working for 300 ms. No signal was passed to createAPIContext: every handler gets one anyway.

questions.q: A caller aborts the call, like a browser tab that was closed. Which should your code check?
questions.explain: The lesson advises checking the code, not the unusual status 499. Codes are meant for programs; messages are meant for people and can change.

questions.q: An admin-only interceptor receives an input that says role: "admin", and the context says the verified role is user. What must happen?
questions.explain: The input is written by the caller. The context is filled by the transport after it verified the caller. Decisions about who may do what use the context only.
options: Allow it, because the input says admin
Refuse it with 403: the role comes only from the context, never from the input
Allow it but log a warning

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Success is 0. Authentication (401) gives 77, validation (422) gives 65, and the conflict (409) falls through to 1. A script can now tell "fix your input" from "sign in" without reading text.

questions.q: Write the result pattern the executor uses. Finish safeDivide(a, b): return { ok: true, data: a / b }, or { ok: false, error: "division by zero" } when b is 0. Never throw. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: A result object makes failure a normal value. The caller checks ok instead of wrapping every call in try/catch, and cannot forget the failure case.
questions.expected:
{ ok: true, data: 2.5 }
{ ok: false, error: 'division by zero' }

questions.q: A handler should stop waiting when its context.signal aborts. Finish sleep(ms, signal): start a timer that resolves after ms, and when signal fires "abort", clear the timer and reject with signal.reason. The program should print the line in the comment.
questions.explain: The signal's "abort" event is the moment to stop. Clearing the timer frees it, and rejecting with signal.reason passes on why, the way the lesson's handler received the APITimeoutError.

questions.q: Finish exitCode(result) for a command-line tool: 0 for success, 77 for status 401 or 403, 65 for 422, and 1 for anything else. The program should print [ 0, 77, 77, 65, 1 ].
questions.explain: Check ok first, then map status codes to exit codes. A script that runs the tool can react to the number without reading any text. This is the CLI transport's translation step.

questions.q: Write your own normalizeId(value, fallback): keep value when it is a string of 1 to 64 characters that only contains letters, digits, -, _ or .; otherwise return fallback. The program should print web-42 fresh-id fresh-id.
questions.explain: An allow-list with ^ and $ checks the whole string, so a line break or a space anywhere fails. A missing header (undefined) gets the fallback too. The real normalizeRequestId uses a fresh UUID as the fallback.

questions.q: Build an interceptor chain by hand. Finish run(interceptors, handler): call the first interceptor with a next function that runs the rest of the chain, and at the end calls handler(). Each interceptor is a function (next) => result. The program should print [ 'log in', 'auth', 'handler', 'log out' ] and then done.
questions.explain: Each step gives its interceptor a next that runs the following step; after the last interceptor comes the handler. That is why the first interceptor in the list is the outermost.

questions.q: Finish the admin check. adminOnly(operation, context, input) returns { ok: false, status: 403 } when the operation's tags include "Admin" and context.role is not "admin". Otherwise it returns { ok: true }. Never look at input. The program should print 403 true true.
questions.explain: Bo's input claims admin, but the verified context says user, so he gets 403. The rule only applies to operations tagged Admin, so Bo can still list tasks.

questions.q: Write a tiny operation registry. Finish register (throw an Error with the message frozen once frozen is true, otherwise store the operation by its name) and freeze. The program should print frozen and then true false.
questions.explain: Freezing after startup means no code can add or replace an operation while requests are running. Register everything first, then freeze.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: get(name) returns undefined when the name is unknown, so the transport can answer 404 itself. require(name) throws an API error with status 404 instead.

questions.q: The queue binding reads the user from the job's metadata. The second job puts userId in its data instead. What does this print?
questions.explain: The job data is the operation's input, not an identity. Only the metadata that your own code wrote after checking the user counts, so the second job reaches requireUser without a user and fails.
options:
completed Water plants
failed Sign in first.

completed Water plants
completed Walk the dog

failed Sign in first.
failed Sign in first.
